levelDescription.value:
By the end of Year 10 students should have had the opportunity to design and produce at least 4 designed solutions focused on one or more of the 4 technologies contexts:

Engineering principles and systems
Food and fibre production
Food specialisations
Materials and technologies specialisations.
Students should have opportunities to experience creating designed solutions for products, services and environments.

Students use design and technologies knowledge and understanding, processes and production skills and design thinking to produce designed solutions for identified needs or opportunities of relevance to individuals and local, regional or global communities. They work independently and collaboratively. Problem-solving activities acknowledge the complexities of contemporary life and make connections to related specialised occupations and further study. Increasingly, study has a global perspective, with opportunities to understand the complex interdependencies involved in the development of technologies and enterprises.

Students specifically focus on preferred futures, taking into account ethics; legal issues; social values; and economic, environmental and social sustainability factors; and use strategies such as life cycle thinking. They use critical thinking, creativity, innovation and enterprise skills with increasing confidence, independence and collaboration. Students analyse data, evaluate design ideas and technologies, respond to feedback, and evaluate design processes used to inform designed solutions for preferred futures.

Using a range of technologies including a variety of graphical representation techniques to communicate, students generate and represent original ideas and production plans in 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional representations. These techniques will be specific to the technologies context and may include scale, perspective, orthogonal and production drawings with sectional and exploded views. Students produce rendered, illustrated views for marketing and use graphic visualisation software to produce dynamic views of design ideas and designed solutions.

Students identify the steps involved in planning the production of designed solutions. They develop detailed project management plans, incorporating elements such as sequenced time, cost and action plans, to manage design tasks safely. Students apply management plans, making adjustments when necessary, to successfully complete design tasks. They identify and establish safety procedures that minimise risk and manage projects with safety and efficiency in mind, maintaining safety standards and management procedures to ensure success.

description.value: In this Year 9 Wood Technology unit, students develop practical woodworking skills by designing and constructing a functional timber paper towel holder. Students learn to accurately measure, mark, cut, shape and assemble timber components using appropriate hand tools, portable power tools and workshop machinery. The project introduces timber-joint applications, including mortise-and-tenon and stopped-housing joints, while emphasising accuracy, fit, strength and quality of finish. Students also investigate existing products, develop personalised design ideas, produce CAD drawings and document the manufacturing process. Workshop safety, risk management, time management and responsible use of materials are reinforced throughout the unit.

Students will design and manufacture an individual wooden paper towel holder based on the supplied working drawing. The finished product must be functional, accurately constructed and include appropriate personalisation or design modifications.

Assessment evidence will include:

A completed timber paper towel holder
A design folio containing a brief, success criteria and constraints
Research and analysis of existing products
Initial ideas and annotated design improvements
A CAD model and dimensioned orthographic drawings
A risk assessment and material cutting list
Photographic documentation of the production process
Evaluation, peer feedback and self-assessment
Associated theory covering workshop safety, abrasives, adhesives, fasteners, finishing processes and woodworking equipment

Students will be assessed on their understanding of tools and production processes, development and communication of design ideas, safe workshop practices, accuracy and quality of construction, application of timber joints, management of production steps and evaluation of the final solution.

conditions.value:
• A timber paper towel holder (constructed prototype).
• A design folio (maximum 10 A4 pages).
• Folio must include: project brief, success criteria, annotated research, CAD model with orthographic projections, risk assessment, material cutting list, process photography, and reflective evaluation.
• Practical construction: demonstrated competency in safe tool operation, joint accuracy, and finishing techniques assessed in the workshop.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students explain how people consider factors that impact on design decisions and the technologies used to design and produce products, services and environments for sustainable living. They explain the contribution of innovation, enterprise skills and emerging technologies to global preferred futures. For one or more of the technologies contexts, students explain the features of technologies and their appropriateness for purpose, and create designed solutions based on an analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create, adapt and refine design ideas, processes and solutions and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. Students independently and collaboratively develop and apply production and project management plans, adjusting processes when necessary. They select and use technologies skilfully and safely to produce designed solutions.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically within the Manual Arts faculty to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum achievement standards. This process includes:

*   **Moderation Conferencing:** Scheduled meetings in Week 5 to review the progress of design folios and evaluate initial CAD representations.
*   **Cross-marking:** Departmental review of final project marking guides prior to the assessment period to ensure the consistent application of criteria regarding joinery accuracy, quality of finish, and safety compliance.
*   **Verification:** Final student work samples are collaboratively reviewed in Week 10 to ensure alignment with the expected achievement standards for Year 10 Design and Technologies.

description.value: In this Year 9 Wood Technology unit, students investigate the precision and craftsmanship required in cabinet and furniture making through the design and construction of a wooden jewellery box. Students develop increasingly sophisticated woodworking skills, with a particular focus on accurate measurement, marking out, hand-tool use and the construction of dovetail joints. They work from a supplied design while incorporating personalised features to make their jewellery box unique. Throughout the unit, students apply workshop safety procedures, select appropriate tools and processes, and document the design and production process in a project folio. The completed product is evaluated for its functionality, appearance, accuracy and overall quality of manufacture.

Students design and manufacture an individual wooden jewellery box based on the supplied specifications. The finished product must be functional, accurately constructed and include appropriate personalisation or decorative features.

Assessment evidence will include:

A completed wooden jewellery box incorporating dovetail joinery
Accurate measurement, marking out, cutting, assembly and finishing
Safe and responsible use of hand tools, power equipment and workshop processes
A project folio containing a design brief, success criteria and constraints
Research and analysis of existing jewellery box designs
A dimensioned design sketch and material cutting list
A completed risk assessment
Documentation and explanation of the production process
An evaluation of the finished product against the design brief and success criteria
Responses to associated theory questions covering workshop safety, timber properties, woodworking joints, tools and production procedures

Students will be assessed on their knowledge and understanding of woodworking processes and their ability to investigate, generate, produce and evaluate a designed solution.

• Supervised workshop sessions for practical construction and safety testing

description.value:
In this Year 9 Wood Technology unit, students develop their woodworking skills by designing and constructing a functional folding camp stool. Students interpret working drawings, accurately measure and mark timber, and manufacture a range of traditional timber joints, including mortise-and-tenon, bridle, housing and dovetail joints. They safely select and use hand tools, portable power tools and workshop equipment while developing accuracy, patience and attention to detail.

Students also complete a folio documenting the design and production process. They investigate existing products, establish a design brief and success criteria, identify constraints, communicate a personalised design, complete a risk assessment and material cutting list, and evaluate the suitability and quality of their finished solution.

Students will design and construct a folding timber camp stool based on the supplied specifications and working drawings. The stool must be functional, stable, accurately assembled and appropriately finished. Students may personalise aspects of the stool, such as the timber details, canvas seat or surface finish.

Assessment evidence will include:

A completed and functional camp stool.
Accurate measurement, marking, cutting and fitting of timber components.
Construction of the specified timber joints.
Safe and appropriate use of hand tools, power tools and workshop equipment.
A design folio containing a design brief, success criteria and constraints.
Research into existing products, supported by an analysis of advantages and disadvantages.
A communicated design with dimensions, materials and annotations.
A risk assessment and material cutting list.
An evaluation of the finished product against the design brief and success criteria.
Completion of associated theory covering workshop safety, materials, CNC technology, coordinates, area calculations and portable power tools.

description.value:
In this unit, students develop woodworking knowledge and practical skills by designing and constructing a personalised timber wall-shelving unit. Students interpret working drawings, prepare a cutting list and use accurate measurement and marking-out techniques to manufacture the project. Construction introduces increasingly sophisticated cabinetmaking joints, including stopped housing joints, mortise-and-tenon joints and dovetail joints. Students also manufacture and fit a small drawer, plywood components and a customised back panel.

Throughout the unit, students safely select and use hand tools, portable power tools and workshop equipment. They investigate timber and manufactured boards, workshop safety, production processes and the characteristics of different materials. Students document the design and production process in a folio and evaluate the functionality, appearance and quality of their completed shelving unit.

Students design and construct a functional timber wall-shelving unit based on the supplied working drawing. The fundamental dimensions and construction methods are provided, but students personalise the project through changes to features such as the back panel, shape, detailing and finish.

Assessment evidence is collected through:

A completed wall-shelving unit demonstrating accurate marking out, joint construction, assembly, drawer fitting, surface preparation and finishing.
A design and production folio containing a design brief, success criteria, constraints, existing-product research, concept sketches, CAD drawings, orthographic views, risk assessment, cutting list and an annotated photographic production record.
An evaluation comparing the completed product against the design brief and success criteria, supported by peer feedback.
Teacher observation of safe workshop practices, correct tool selection, time management and practical skill.
Associated theory activities covering workshop safety, timber and manufactured boards, emerging materials, hand tools and portable power tools.

• Folio: 6–8 A4 pages or equivalent digital media, including CAD drawings, cutting lists, and production records
• Final product: A functional wall-shelving unit completed to design specifications
• Supervised classroom conditions for theory and safety testing

description.value:
In this Year 10 Wood Technology unit, students design and manufacture a timber footstool based on a supplied design. Students develop practical woodworking skills while learning how accurate measurement, timber preparation, joint construction and careful finishing contribute to a functional and aesthetically pleasing furniture product. The project allows students to personalise the supplied design through considered changes to its form, materials or appearance.

Throughout the unit, students use hand tools, portable power tools and workshop machinery while following established risk-control procedures. They investigate existing products, develop and communicate design ideas, produce a CAD model and document the manufacture of their footstool in a design folio. Particular emphasis is placed on accuracy, biscuit-joint construction, attention to detail, safe working practices and evaluating the quality of the completed product.

Students are required to design and manufacture an innovative and personalised timber footstool that meets the specifications of the supplied project drawing. The practical product should demonstrate accurate marking and measuring, appropriate use of tools and machinery, close-fitting joints, effective assembly and a high-quality surface finish.

Students will also complete an individual design and production folio containing:

A design brief, success criteria and project constraints
Research and analysis of three existing footstools
An initial design and three proposed modifications
An annotated final design
A CAD model and dimensioned orthographic drawings
A risk assessment
A material cutting list and project costing
A photographic production record
An evaluation and peer evaluation
Associated theory covering workshop safety, abrasive grades, PVA adhesive, biscuit joints, pilot and clearance holes, and relevant tools and machinery

Assessment evidence will be gathered from the completed footstool, design folio, associated theory work, teacher observation and safe workshop participation.

conditions.value:

• Physical timber footstool (maximum dimension: 450mm x 450mm x 450mm)
• Individual design folio to be submitted in digital or hard-copy format
• Supervised workshop time for practical construction
• Adherence to WHS procedures and St Brendan’s College workshop safety protocols

Internal moderation is conducted systematically across the Year 10 Technology department to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum achievement standards. This process involves:

description.value: In this unit, students design and construct a timber bedside table using a supplied project drawing as the basis for their work. Students develop their knowledge of furniture construction, timber selection, accurate measurement and the use of timber joints, including mortise and tenon joints. They personalise the supplied design through considered changes to its appearance or features and use CAD to communicate their final design. Throughout the unit, students safely use hand tools, power tools and workshop equipment to produce an accurate, functional and aesthetically pleasing product. Students document the design and production process in a folio and evaluate the quality of their finished bedside table.

Students will individually design and construct a personalised timber bedside table based on the supplied specifications. The finished product must be functional, accurately manufactured and demonstrate appropriate use of timber joints, tools, equipment and finishing processes.

Students will also complete a design folio containing:

Design brief, success criteria and project constraints
Research into existing bedside tables, including advantages and disadvantages
Initial sketches and three proposed design modifications
A CAD model with labelled and dimensioned orthographic views
Risk assessment and control measures
Materials cutting list and project costing
Photographic production procedure with annotations
Evaluation against the design brief and success criteria
Peer and self-evaluation
Associated theory questions about tools, equipment and timber joints

Assessment evidence will be collected through the completed bedside table, design folio, theory responses, teacher observations and the student’s consistent application of safe workshop practices.

• Consistent application of safe work practices and personal protective equipment (PPE) required throughout the production phase.

description.value: In this Year 10 Wood Technology unit, students design and manufacture a personalised timber wall clock based on a supplied project design. Students develop their ability to accurately measure, mark, cut, shape and join timber while using a range of hand tools, portable power tools and workshop machinery. They investigate timber joints, adhesives, surface preparation and clear finishing techniques to produce a functional and visually appealing product. Throughout the unit, students apply workshop safety procedures, manage their time and document the design and production process in a project folio.

Students design and manufacture an individual timber wall clock that meets the supplied dimensions and construction requirements while incorporating their own design modifications and personalisation. The completed clock must be functional, accurately assembled, appropriately finished and produced using safe workshop practices.

Students also submit a project folio containing:

A design brief, success criteria and constraints
Research into three existing clock designs, including advantages and disadvantages
Initial sketches and three proposed modifications
An annotated final design and CAD model
A risk assessment
A materials cutting list and project costing
Photographic evidence and an annotated production procedure
Responses to associated theory questions
A final product evaluation, peer evaluation and self-assessment

Assessment evidence is gathered from the completed clock, the folio and teacher observations of students’ practical skills, safety, tool selection, accuracy and application of production processes.

description.value: In this Year 10 Wood Technology unit, students design and manufacture a personalised timber wall mirror. They investigate existing products, develop and communicate design ideas using sketches and CAD, and select appropriate materials, tools and production processes. Throughout the unit, students apply workshop safety procedures, manage their time and document the development and manufacture of their mirror in a design folio.

Students will design and construct an innovative and aesthetically pleasing timber wall mirror based on the supplied project specifications. The completed mirror must demonstrate accurate construction, close-fitting joints, careful finishing and appropriate personalisation.

A design brief, success criteria and project constraints

Initial sketches and proposed design modifications

Photographic evidence and an annotated production sequence
Responses to associated woodworking theory questions
A final evaluation and peer evaluation

Students will be assessed on their knowledge of tools, materials, production processes and safety, as well as their ability to generate, produce and evaluate a functional designed solution.
